243| \begin{example}[Tuning a radio]\label{ex:b1:sinusoidal-impedance:radio}
244| A coil $L = \qty{200}{\micro H}$ and a variable capacitor: $C =
245| \qty{127}{pF}$ tunes $f_0 = \qty{1.00}{MHz}$. With the coil's wire
246| resistance $R = \qty{12.6}{\ohm}$, $L\omega_0 = \qty{1257}{\ohm}$ and
247| $Q = 100$: bandwidth $\Delta f = f_0/Q = \qty{10}{kHz}$ --- the width of
248| an AM channel --- and the \qty{10}{\micro V} induced by a distant
249| transmitter become $QE = \qty{1}{mV}$ across the capacitor, free of
250| charge. The weekend problem builds this receiver.
251| \end{example}

253| \begin{remark}[Why $Q$ again]\label{rem:b1:sinusoidal-impedance:Q}
254| The $Q$ of this chapter is the $Q$ of \cref{ch:b1:transient-regimes}:
255| the circuit that rings for about $Q$ oscillations when struck is the
256| one that resonates over a band $\omega_0/Q$ wide when driven. Both
257| express one ratio: $2\pi$ times the energy stored over the energy
258| dissipated per period (\cref{exo:b1:sinusoidal-impedance:12}). A
259| sharp resonance and a long ringing are the same property, and so is the
260| slow response: a filter of bandwidth $\Delta\omega$ takes a time of
261| order $1/\Delta\omega$ to settle.
262| \end{remark}

264| \section{Power in the sinusoidal regime}
265| 
266| \begin{definition}[RMS value]\label{def:b1:sinusoidal-impedance:rms}
267| \index{rms value}\index{effective value}
268| The \emph{root-mean-square} (rms, or effective) value of a periodic
269| signal $x(t)$ is $X_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\langle x^2\rangle}$, the
270| square root of the time average of $x^2$ over a period. For a sinusoid
271| of amplitude $X$, $X_{\mathrm{rms}} = X/\sqrt2$. The \qty{230}{V} of the
272| mains is an rms value; its amplitude is \qty{325}{V}.
273| \end{definition}
274| 
275| \begin{theorem}[Average power]\label{thm:b1:sinusoidal-impedance:power}
276| \index{average power}\index{power factor}\index{reactive power}
277| A dipole with $u = U\cos\omega t$ and $i = I\cos(\omega t - \varphi)$
278| (receiver convention) receives the instantaneous power $p = ui$, of
279| average
280| \[
281| P = \tfrac12\,UI\cos\varphi = U_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}\cos\varphi
282| = \tfrac12\Rea\!\big(\underline U\,\underline I^{\,*}\big) = \tfrac12\Rea(\underline Z)\,I^2,
283| \]
284| where $\cos\varphi$ is the \emph{power factor}. A resistor receives
285| $\tfrac12 RI^2 = RI_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$; an ideal coil or capacitor
286| ($\varphi = \pm\pi/2$) receives no average power --- it stores energy
287| during half a period and returns it during the other half.
288| \end{theorem}
289| 
290| \begin{proof}
291| $p = UI\cos\omega t\cos(\omega t - \varphi) = \tfrac12 UI[\cos\varphi +
292| \cos(2\omega t - \varphi)]$; the second term averages to zero. With
293| $\underline U = U$ and $\underline I = I\eu^{-j\varphi}$,
294| $\underline U\,\underline I^* = UI\eu^{j\varphi}$, whose real part is
295| $UI\cos\varphi$; and $\underline U = \underline Z\,\underline I$ gives
296| $\underline U\,\underline I^* = \underline Z I^2$.
297| \end{proof}

318| \begin{example}[Power factor correction]\label{ex:b1:sinusoidal-impedance:pf}
319| A workshop motor on \qty{230}{V} rms draws \qty{2.0}{kW} with
320| $\cos\varphi = 0.70$ (inductive): $I_{\mathrm{rms}} = 2000/(230 \times
321| 0.70) = \qty{12.4}{A}$, against \qty{8.7}{A} if the power factor were
322| $1$ --- the extra current heats the utility's cables for nothing, hence
323| the penalty. A capacitor in parallel supplies the coil's quarter-period
324| energy swings locally: the \emph{reactive power} $P\tan\varphi =
325| \qty{2.0}{kvar}$ needs $C = P\tan\varphi/(\omega U_{\mathrm{rms}}^2)
326| \approx \qty{120}{\micro F}$ at \qty{50}{Hz}, and the line current drops
327| to \qty{8.7}{A}.
328| \end{example}
